utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, if I may just comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday I had indicated that I wanted to cite an assertion I made or give citations for it. Having reviewed the transcript, it seems that what is recorded in the transcript is not what I intended to say, and not what I thought said. And I presume that that the transcript is probably right. What I thought I said was that the accused had said that he was in Kosovo in 1998 when he testified. I think the transcript has me saying that this witness said that the accused was in Kosovo in 1998. So the citations I have of the accused saying he was in Kosovo, according to the transcript, that is not what was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that very neat recovery. And I think a brownie point for Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Stamp, you are continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown a few of the orders or dispatches signed by General Djordjevic in which he mobilised and dispatched PJP detachments in Kosovo. Perhaps we can have a look at one or two of them quickly. You were shown P133. This is a dispatch of 28th of July, 1998. And if you turn to the second page, you see it's signed by -- it's signed for the chief of the public security department General Djordjevic, and you were also shown a couple of the documents in which General Djordjevic mobilised and dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could go back to the first page of this document, that would be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were also shown a couple of documents in which General Djordjevic mobilised and dispatched these PJP units from various SUPs in Serbia to Djordjevic -- to Kosovo and Metohija. Under what authority did he issue these orders? And specifically if you look at the first line of this order, that these detachments are to be mobilised and dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are dispatches of the chief of the public security department of the Ministry of the Interior which were sent to the secretariats whereby the units were to be sent to carry out special security tasks in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Here the 65th Detachment is also mentioned. This is the detachment in which one of my units was, this was the company size unit of approximately 100 people. So with this dispatch, he addressed the secretariats so that they prepared their units in order to send them to carry out special security tasks. He sent this as chief of public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. He sent this detachment mobilising, dispatching these PJP units to carry out security tasks in Kosovo. I am sorry, I see the transcript has something wrong. He sent this dispatch by which he mobilised and dispatched PJP units or carried out special tasks, special security tasks in Kosovo, and he did so as chief of the public security department. Was there any law, rule, or regulation by virtue of which he performed or issued this order?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was issued pursuant to the authorities given by the Ministry of the Interior. This was not in line with any legislation. This is not something that exists neither in the law nor in any other regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said it was issued pursuant to the authorities given by the minister of interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In which case could we look at P58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we have a mistake in the transcript concerning what Mr. Stamp said. I believe that Mr. Stamp said it in the same way in which -- in which the witness said, that this was the authority of the minister -- yes, yes, now it's okay in the transcript, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the decision of 19th of February, 1992, setting out the PJM -- sorry, it's a decision of the 1st of August, 1992 -- 1993, setting out the PJM. You had indicated, just for clarification, Mr. Pantelic, earlier, that there's a name change. The PJM became known as the PJP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These units changed names but their purpose was not changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we see them referred here in this order or referred to here in this order as a PJM. That is what later on became known as a PJP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at the second page of this in English, and you could probably stay on the first page in B/C/S. We want to see item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It says that bringing into readiness, mobilising, and engaging the PJM on performing tasks described in paragraph 1 of this item shall be done on orders from the minister and when approved by the minister, also on orders from the chief of the public security department. So can I take it then that General Djordjevic in issuing these orders, like the last one we saw where he mobilised and dispatched these units to Kosovo for security-related tasks, was done by virtue of this regulation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear so pursuant to this decision because here we can see that putting units into readiness, their mobilisation and engaging of PJMs was done exclusively on orders from the minister or on orders from somebody authorised by the minister to do so, in this case the chief of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, that is not precise what it says. It says either the minister or on the authority of the minister, the chief of the public security department. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this very well under item 2, paragraph 2 within item 2, and here it says on orders from the minister and when approved by the minister, also on orders from the chief of the public security department. This is what this decision reads. So the decision was adopted by the minister and then operational and technical tasks are actually carried out by the chief of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we could move on. Did you have units in Kosovo in mid-April 1999? If I may rephrase. Were there any PJP detachments from your SUP engaged in security-related tasks in Kosovo in mid-April 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of 1999 my units were permanently dispatched to carry out special security tasks in the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija. I can't precisely remember whether in mid-April any such units were there, but it is very probable that they were. So I can't remember the exact dates, but I do know that my company of the PJP was engaged in special security tasks, then there would be a break, and after a short while they would go again. So this was done continuously during the year of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your company belonged to which detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had several companies. These were the third companies of the 35th, 65th, and 85th Detachment. In the 85th Detachment, we mostly had members of the reserve police forces, and they were seldomly used during this period, I even believe they weren't used at all, but members of the 35th Detachment and of the 65th Detachment were used continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have a look at document 06063. This is one that -- that's Prosecution 65 ter number 06063.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the first page at the bottom. This is a document listing the deployment of PJP units on the 17th of April, 1999. The first page at the bottom we see the units of the 35th Detachment, and if we go to the second page in English, and I think we could stay on the same page in B/C/S, we see the 3rd Company at Vaganica. Is that where your -- where the unit from your SUP was located? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is written so in this document, this is certainly correct. So the 35th Detachment of the PJP consisted of police units from Sabac, Valjevo, and Uzice. Their base was in Uzice. So if this is what is written here that the 35th Detachment was deployed at the time, this is most probably true. But I can't remember any details, and I do not know of a place called Vaganica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, this is -- if we go back to page 1 in English. This is in the Secretariat of Kosovska Mitrovica. Did you have units in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PJP's Special Police units of the secretariat from Valjevo spent a longer period of time in the territory of the Secretariat of Kosovska Mitrovica. In 1998 we had one person killed of the PJPs who carried out security tasks of the protection of a hunting ammunition factory in Srbica. Thereafter, during the course of 1999 on several occasions, members of this detachment of PJP were present in the territory which was under the jurisdiction of the secretariat from Mitrovica. On the 26th of March, while carrying out security tasks in that territory, so I'm talking about the 26th of March, 1999, when entering the village of Lajkovac, five members of my unit were killed and six of them were heavily injured. On that occasion, they were carrying out the tasks that were ordered to them by the Pristina staff and the Secretariat of the Interior in Mitrovica. They controlled the terrain in the given area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. You had explained that to us yesterday. If we look at item 2 on the Secretariat for Kosovska Mitrovica, and that is on the second page in English, we see their deployments or deployment of the units in the 85th detachment. Do you see where the 3rd -- or the areas where the 3rd Company is deployed? Did you have any units deployed in those areas?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember whether at the time any of my units were sent down there because we never had a full detachment. It depended on the security situation, so it was requested for particular secretariats, and as I told you a short while ago, these were three secretariats, in Uzice, Sabac, and Valjevo, to provide a certain number of men. This doesn't necessarily mean that a full company from the secretariat in Valjevo was deployed to the detachment. I honestly cannot remember the dates and whether this was the case at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see that this document is of more significant interest of Mr. Stamp, so I would first of all like to hear what is this all about, possibly we first had to see whether the witness could recognise this document, and there is no introduction into the document, no signatures, so we do know where it comes from. I do not mind the questions that my learned friend asked, but I wonder whether we could establish what is this document all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As far as I know, this is not yet an exhibit, is that so, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I'm merely asking the witness whether he knows whether the information on it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you intending on exhibiting the document at some later time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you want it marked or identification at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That had been my plan, that was my intention depending on his answers, which the answers being as they are, that would be the course of conduct I would pursue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01545, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You kept, I think it is your evidence, regular contact with your men, your men who had been assigned to Kosovo by way of telephone calls. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I was in contact with them possibly every four to five days depending on the situation, depending on the area in which they were deployed, and depending on whether they could use any secured phone lines to call me and inform me about their problems and possible assistance that I could have provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this situation continued throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean throughout the war, but occasionally it would happen that we couldn't talk to one another for ten days, but what was important for me was that they were all alive and well, that nobody was killed or injured, and that they held all the conditions necessary to perform their tasks normally in the territory in which they were employed to carry out security tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When I said during the war, I mean during the period of the NATO intervention in 1999. Did you maintain contact with your units in Kosovo during this period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time ago, but when I had an opportunity, I would use it, so either the commanders of the units deployed in Kosovo got in touch with me somehow, but as I said, this was not continuously. So we spoke occasionally; I received information; and this was sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll try to ask the question in a different way. During the war, during the NATO intervention, did you have any contact at all with your men in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the NATO intervention, the contacts were very far apart, but we still spoke. I can't remember how many times a month or a week, but if I couldn't get in touch with any of them, then I would call the staff in Pristina, and I would ask about them. And this was enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you could more readily get in touch with the staff in Pristina than your units that were in the field outside of Pristina; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in touch with the staff in Pristina occasionally until NATO aircraft struck the facility where the staff had been housed. Later on when it was dispatched to reserve positions, I basically had no contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About when was it that NATO struck their position?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when NATO attacked the territory of the municipality of Valjevo. As for Kosovo, I know that it was bombed on a daily basis, and that facility was probably struck at the outset. As for any dates, I don't know those, and I can't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that when your PJP detachments went down to Kosovo, then you had no further responsibility to monitor them and to maintain disciplinary control of them. That responsibility resided in the secretariats to which they were sent. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the moment when PJP units were sent from the territory of our secretariat where I was the chief, all my obligations towards those PJP units ceased. What I had to do was to use the -- an inspector from the department of police to have him organise their departure in keeping with the dispatch I received from the police administration of the Ministry of the Interior. I had to provide them with everything requested in that dispatch, and as of the moment when they left the territory of my secretariat, I no longer had any competencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this question it was put to the witness that he said something he didn't actually say. He said previously that he had no disciplinary oversight over those units. Mr. Stamp referred to something of that sort, and I would perhaps like to know what the reference is that he is relying upon, otherwise perhaps the question should be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I asked the witness if he said something, and he explained what he meant. But it seemed that my friend doesn't understand the question I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, was this procedure, the one you just described, where you lost any competency over the units that were sent, was that something that was regulated by law or by the rules?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That issue was not regulated by any legal provisions. However, it is regulated by a number of bylaws put into force by the minister of the interior. Perhaps I should clarify the issue of disciplinary measures. In cases of infringement of the disciplinary rules from the disciplinary code committed in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija by members of the PJP who had been sent to that area, their immediate superior had to establish whether there was any disciplinary liability. In such cases, he was charged with undertaking measures, preliminary measures, after which he was supposed to forward the case file to the home secretariat. So the preliminary measures were under the competence of the immediate superior, and once those who breached discipline returned to their home secretariat, proceedings would be instituted against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. So when it came to disciplinary matters at least, the home secretariat did retain some competence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The home secretariat had that sole competence in cases of disciplinary liability. In such cases, the employee would be held accountable upon his return to the home secretariat. Otherwise, the home secretariat held no sway in any other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 0 -- that is 65 ter number 05234. This was a document that we -- was not on our initial notification, but we notified the Defence as soon as there was testimony that caused us to believe the witness might be able to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in. This actually confirms what I have just said. In the last paragraph it reads that for the above-mentioned reasons, it is proposed that the person concerned be temporarily removed from the ministry until the date mentioned therein. So the chief of secretariat was instructed to undertake disciplinary measures concerning this case. The person in question was not suspended, but sent to his home unit and home secretariat so as to have disciplinary measures imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. There -- just to be accurate, this is the Chief of Secretariat of Bor, SUP Bor, Caslav Golubovic seeking approval to bring disciplinary charges against a MUP employee for breaches committed in Kosovo; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, as we can read from the document. However, the chief of secretariat, by that time in 1999 was probably not familiar with how disciplinary proceedings were regulated at the time and where they were supposed to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am afraid I don't understand your last comment. Are you saying that what SUP chief Golubovic is doing here is irregular?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say what he was doing was irregular. I'm just saying that I don't know why he asked the minister of the interior of Serbia for an approval to be in charge of such a procedure. In the earlier dispatches we saw, the whole situation was well regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At that time, the 23rd of March, 1999, would he not have to seek the permission of the administration in Belgrade, the headquarters in Belgrade to remove the officer from the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chiefs of the SUP who signed this asked for approval to suspend the employee pending the closure proceedings. So that person was not sent away. He was simply returned to his home unit and to the home secretariat from which he had been dispatched. The reason for which the secretariat chief was inquiring of the Serbian MUP what to do, that is something that I'm not very clear about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you don't know whether or not at that time the SUP chief would have to request permission from MUP headquarters to remove a MUP employee from his employment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just said, I explained to you how I conducted military procedures in the territory of my SUP. I wasn't aware of any need to have the approval of the MUP of Serbia for such measures. Although, to speak honestly, I did not have any disciplinary cases on my hands on which I had to act. As far as I remember, though, no approval on the part of the ministry would have been necessary for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document, 5234, and ask that it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01546.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move on. Could we look at P1207.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said yesterday that by this dispatch, General Djordjevic issued regular tasks to various departments and organisational units of the police. You see in the addressee section, Mr. Pantelic, that one of the organisational unit was the "UKP, the Crime Police Administration - here - to the chief."?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is hardly legible. Yes, now I see it. It was sent to the UKP by the sector chief. These are tasks passed down along certain professional lines, and I have no information regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The chief of the crime police was General Ilic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that at least for some purposes the hierarchy remained in place, General Djordjevic could and did task General Ilic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do is confirm what the dispatch says. It was sent to the chief of administration. I don't know for what reasons and why. As I have said, it was my impression that General Ilic was directly subordinated to the minister of the interior, and I stand by that assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suppose you have answered the question. For clarification, I think you said that these were tasks passed down along the professional lines, and I'm saying to you doesn't this demonstrate that General Djordjevic could and did task General Ilic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he could issue orders only following the minister's approval, strictly speaking. Following the rule book, the minister would not be involved in this. As of 1987 [as interpreted] when assistant ministers of the interior were appointed, each of them answered for a certain aspect of work --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But we have heard about the history. I just want to confine ourselves to this document and what you have said about it in your testimony. And on the basis of that, would it be fair to say that General Djordjevic as chief of the public security sector could and did issue tasks to General Ilic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered. In any case, this dispatch --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my answer that following a minister's approval, he could issue any type of dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So that is a hierarchy. The minister is superior to General Djordjevic; General Djordjevic is superior to General Ilic; General Ilic is superior to the UKP chiefs in the SUPs. There is a hierarchy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hierarchy, as you describe it, is correct only in the first part of your question. General Ilic was not subordinated to the territorial units. His tasks were to exercise direct co-ordination and control of work following which he could undertake certain measures in the criminal or crime area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There must have been an error. I wasn't suggesting that General Ilic was subordinated to the territorial units. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. A correction for the transcript. Page 15, line 8, it is 1987, whereas I believe the witness said 1997. I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Stamp, but having realised that he is finished with this topic, I made use of this opportunity to point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on and have a look quickly at P356.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a dispatch from General Djordjevic of the 18th of February, 1999, that you spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move straight to item 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were saying, Mr. Pantelic -- or let me put it this way. Your understanding, is it that when he referred to volunteers, it meant that volunteers were to be directed towards your appropriate military territorial unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the appropriate military territorial unit. Under the existing Law on the Interior, no volunteers can be engaged in the execution of any security-related tasks. They could -- such people could only have come from the reserve force of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And are you also saying that when he was referring to the paramilitary units and their members, he meant the suppression of paramilitary units and their members because they were inclined to include criminal elements?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think one needs to generalise. For the most part, units did contain criminal elements, but there were different units as well. Specifically in my area, there were no paramilitary units. I didn't register a single one, and I didn't notify the minister of the interior of the existence of any such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could go back to the first page of that document just to get the reference number or the dispatch number. Dispatch number 312, dated 18th of February, 1999. Now if we could move to P702.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I just want to remind you of what you said yesterday about paramilitaries. It's at 12079, line 7: "I believe the law on people's Defence did not regulate paramilitary units. Usually these were people who came from the rank of criminals, and we tried in every way we could to eliminate them partaking in any kind of volunteer units." So please remember your testimony. You will see in this document, this is a dispatch of the 24th of March, 1999. We'll see later that it is from the minister, that is Mr. Djordjevic's superior, and you see in the first paragraph it says or refers to "our dispatch number 312 of the 18th of February, 1999," that's the previous dispatch you just saw. Just read that first paragraph, please. Not aloud, just read it so you understand it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I can't read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, if it could be expanded, and I'll read it to you in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It says: "Since the 23rd of March" ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go back to the English, and go to page 3 of the English and ... I am sorry, I think we want page 2 of the English. Now, I don't have a copy in front of me. I think we need page 1 then. I'm so sorry. Yes, item 5 of page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Here, the minister on the eve of the war is telling us, "you shall" -- and I quote: "You shall register all volunteer and paramilitary units and their members and keep them under control in case you might need to engage them." Do you know that it was the intention of the minister and General Djordjevic to illegally engage volunteers into the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the then law on the Internal Affairs, no volunteers could be engaged in units that were under the command of the Ministry of the Interior on any of the their organisational units. What is written here in this dispatch that they should be kept under control and what the exact intention of the minister were regarding this particular dispatch, I cannot comment on that. As I said a short while ago, in my territory, in the territory under my jurisdiction, there were no such units and there was no need to keep them under control or to inform the ministry about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question asked you about the purpose of the minister and General Djordjevic in respect to the volunteers. I take it your answer is, you don't know, having seen this. Can I ask you in respect to the paramilitaries, did you know or were you aware that it was the intention of the minister and General Djordjevic to engage paramilitary units, people who usually came from the ranks of criminals, to quote your words, into the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure how I could comment on this. This is the first time that I have learned that there was any intention to engage such units as members of the Ministry of the Interior. We never discussed this at any of the meetings or during any of the conversations with the generals and representatives of different professional lines at the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware of a meeting attended by General Djordjevic, the minister, General Lukic, and the leaders of the police from Kosovo and Metohija on the 17th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that meeting could have been all about, but probably by the nature of things, I was not supposed to know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if you recall the first document on this topic you were shown, that is, General Djordjevic's dispatch of the 18th of February, 1999, it included the matters that were discussed at the meeting of the 17th of February. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that dispatch unless I'm reminded of it, but what happened away from the territory of my secretariat, I had very little knowledge on that, and I will gladly share with you those things that I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but I'm mostly interested right now in matters relating to Kosovo. If we could move on. The Law on Internal Affairs remained in force during the NATO intervention, did to not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It remained in force and also the decree on the Internal Affairs during a state of war was implemented. The one that was adopted by the federal government, and if there were any colliding provisions, then the decree was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could just take things in chronological order or step by step. There was also in force a decree on disciplinary responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is P1049. Perhaps the witness could have a look at it just to orient himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This decree on disciplinary responsibility in the Ministry of the Interior, that was also in force during the NATO intervention, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this decree simply precised the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at Article 8 of that decree. Paragraph 2 of Article 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is in respect to proceedings for serious breaches, and in paragraph 2 indicates that "... for serious breaches which constitute a crime, disciplinary investigator shall interview the employee witnesses and expert witnesses, collect the evidence, and investigate ex-officio all circumstance of significance for the full determination of responsibility." That was the -- or one of the operational provisions, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the Article 9 provides that: "The immediate supervisor shall report any serious breaches to the responsible officer." And just so that we can be sure where we are, could we look at Article 4 for who is the responsible officer. Chief of the secretariat, chief of the administration, or other appropriate organisational unit at the headquarters of the ministry. Those are the persons who would institute the disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Disciplinary proceedings were launched following a report which was filed by the immediately superior officer. We have to distinguish between two things. First of all a disciplinary report and a disciplinary proceedings and issuing of disciplinary measures. In the previous articles that we saw a short while ago, it was stipulated that in case of a disciplinary offence which constituted a crime, you also had a disciplinary investigator involved who would carry on the proceedings. So if you had a major breach of working discipline without a crime, then the proceedings would have been different, but always the immediately superior person would file a report, that report would reach the chief of the secretariat, and he would forward it to the disciplinary court which decided on the case in the first instance. And in this article which you presented to me, you can see that it was possible to appeal, so both parties could appeal that court decision. So the person against whom the disciplinary measure was pronounced, and also the chief who filed this report, but it is important to make this distinction, regardless of the fact whether there were disciplinary proceedings and also criminal proceedings or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have just described the -- how criminal proceedings would be instituted for serious breaches that constituted a crime. Weren't the powers of the security organs, the MUP, expanded during the war? In other words, weren't SUP chiefs or the responsible officer that we see here given expanded powers to investigate crimes and arrest and detain persons?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have two issues. The decree on the Internal Affairs during a state of war also regulated disciplinary responsibility of employees, and it provided for more expanded powers, so following the authorisation of the head of the unit given to the chiefs of territorial organisational units, they could carry out proceedings for serious breaches of discipline during a state of war, and they could also pronounce appropriate measures. The second issue is related to the law on the application of criminal proceedings during a state of war. According to that law, on the application of criminal proceedings, certain powers were also given to the organs of the Ministry of the Interior so that during the state of war, they could carry out some investigative activities without a prosecutor. But they were obliged to report about any such investigative activities that were undertaken, to report to the prosecutor in the shortest possible period of time. So these were interviews with witnesses, opening of letters, and similar actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, let's look at it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P200, please. This is a decree on implementation of criminal procedure during the war. And if we could look at Article 6, paragraphs 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This, I think, confirms what you were saying. Paragraph 3 provides that: "The organ of the interior may in urgent cases carry out investigative activities even without the decision of the public or state prosecutor." In other words, MUP officials could institute investigations and were not hampered by the presence or absence of investigative judges or prosecutors where urgency of the situation required it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely what it means, but you have to understand the conditions under which we worked. The bombs fell throughout the day. There were many casualties. And prosecutors and investigative judges were continuously carrying out crime scene investigations because of different accidents. So under such circumstances, the organs of the interior could not function. Possibly in certain areas they could, but in certain areas they would not be able to function if they were to wait for the prosecutor and investigative judge. Then all the traces would have been lost, and it would be difficult to establish whether this was a crime or a smaller offence, whether this was a general crime offence or disruption of law and order, and so on. So the organs of the interior had to be as efficient as possible and for those reasons, as far as I know, such powers were given to them. However, I can claim with full responsibility that in the territory that was under jurisdiction of my secretariat, these powers were never abused.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. I am not claiming that you or anybody working under your supervision abused powers. I'm just asking the operation or the intended operation of the law. If could you look at paragraph 8 or Article 8 of this. It also gives organs of the interior powers to detain persons.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, in other words, the responsible officers of the interior could or were empowered to launch their own investigations if they had information about crimes being committed, and arrest and detain suspects?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't define it with precisely those words. Members of the Ministry of the Interior even previously had the powers, even before this decree came into force, to arrest persons, interview them, and detain them for a period of up to three days. So with this decree, the powers were simply extended in terms of the time-limit, so now they could detain them for up to 30 days, but it was in nobody's interest to detain suspects for such a long period. If I remember it well, somewhere in this law you can see that they were obliged to immediately send them to carry out their sentences, their penalties in the responsible detention institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next law you mention which is of interest to us was the decree in respect to disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at P1050. This is a 9th of April, 1999, letter by General Djordjevic. I said the next law I mention was the decree in respect to disciplinary measures; I meant the decree on Internal Affairs, which this dispatch from General Djordjevic deals with. Can we look at page 2 in English. And I think it's also page 2 in the B/C/S. Top of the page in both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, just for the purposes of the record, can you read aloud, so we could have an independent translation, the paragraph that states that the chief of the department of public security has authorised the heads. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read that aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The chief of public security sector has authorised the heads of organisational units to impose prescribed measures and punishment for major violations of employment obligations and duties. And this authorisation is enclosed herewith."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I ask you to read this because yesterday I think you said that he authorised the heads of the territorial units, but this, I think you will agree with me, referred to the heads of the organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you understood this well. What I said yesterday was true. He authorised the heads of organisational units. The organisational units existed at the level of the Ministry of the Interior, but there were also organisational territorial units, and these were the secretariats. So the organisational units existed both at the seat of the ministry and in the territory of the entire republic. So all the heads were authorised starting from chiefs of administrations to chiefs of secretariats which are territorial organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. It must be my mistake. I thought yesterday you were limiting this authorisation to the territorial units. So he was authorising organisational units including the crime police headed by General Ilic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says those in charge of organisational units, he had in mind the chiefs of all administrations within the Ministry of the Interior. Dragan Ilic, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say from the authorisation here that General Djordjevic was entitled to grant to the organisational units that he was a professional police officer most responsible for the enforcement of discipline in the MUP during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document we are looking at stemming from the decree on Internal Affairs during a state of war provided certain authority to the organs of the interior, and it had to be abided by. Someone signing this dispatch, and later on we see a similar dispatch, signed by the chief of joint affairs administration of the ministry, which was also forwarded to all organisational units - I think we discussed that yesterday - is more precise in terms of what the chief of the sector signed in this document. By virtue of this decree, the chief of the sector had to address such a document to all organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree with me that by virtue of the decree, it was invested in the chief of the public security sector the power and the right to authorise the heads of organisational units to impose the sentences? He was invested with that power, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such an authorisation could have only come from the minister. As to who he delegated the powers to see that implemented, that's no longer an issue of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you were given this document to comment upon earlier on when you testified in chief, and you commented upon it on the basis that you received it and you are aware of its meaning and purpose. It says clearly here that: "For serious violations of obligations and duty, the chief of the ministry department or a person he authorises, shall impose measures and punishments as proposed by the immediate superior." And that's quotation. Then General Djordjevic goes on and issues his authorisation: "The chief of the department of public security has authorised the heads of organisational units to impose prescribed measures and sentences ..." Wouldn't you agree with me that General Djordjevic had the right and the power to authorise the heads of the organisational units both in Belgrade and in the territorial units to impose sentences for serious breaches?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, this was delegated pursuant to a decision by the minister. Chief Djordjevic addressed the organisational units forwarding to them the decision of the Government of Serbia. I can tell you once again that this decree was practically not implemented during the state of war. You won't find even two or three secretariats in which at the time it was being implemented. I don't think there's any reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you are going way beyond the question I'm asking you because -- and more. You are telling us thing that even you said you didn't know. You don't know what is going on in Kosovo, you said that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it not fair to say that if you take the minister out of this equation, and the minister is, I think we can agree with each other, the person in charge of the ministry. Wouldn't you agree with me that General Djordjevic was the highest professional officer in the MUP charged with and responsible for the enforcement of discipline in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this dispatch as it reads, I could agree with you you. However, he delegated that responsibility to the chiefs of other organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have two more minutes, five more minutes, but perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: After the break, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the break now and resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you said when you were here last time, or yesterday, that to speak of a plan to expel the Kosovo Albanians was absurd. I'd like to show you a video, just a small clip and ask you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is P1510, Your Honours, that we notified a little bit late because of what the witness said in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that it's not quite so absurd to suggest. Or may I ask you this question, did you know that Mr. Seselj made this speech shortly before the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj said many things. I don't recall these words specifically, but I do know that he frequently appeared in the media saying things which one wouldn't say are shared by all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was he a member of the government at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for a while he was a government official, but I don't recall what year it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there a deputy prime minister during 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Briefly before I embark upon my redirect which will last five minutes at the most, I just wanted to point out this fact, the last video-clip we saw was the fourth document shown to this witness which he had no occasion to see during his proofing with the Defence. This is the fourth document that was disclosed to the Defence in the course of this witness's testimony. I don't think the Prosecutor showed more than seven or eight documents during this witness's cross, out of which basically half of that number were given to us during his testimony. I didn't want to raise this issue before so as not to interrupt the testimony, but I think this type of conduct on the part of the Prosecutor points to the existence of a pattern. These were no longer individual instances. I will now resume my redirect. MR. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, before you pass quickly off the point, part of the problem with this particular witness is that his evidence was given viva voce. It was not given on the basis of a prepared statement. For that reason, it is, I would suggest to you, not easy to anticipate all that the witness may say in the course of his evidence. I think you need to bear that in mind because if you think over the evidence of the previous witnesses, it has not been a common occurrence for a document to be used in cross-examination without proper prior notification. There have been instances, those instances have, I think, been less than was the case of the Defence when cross-examining Prosecution witnesses. But this witness has this great difference that much of his evidence is something that the Prosecution may not anticipate in its particulars. Therefore, when it is heard what the witness says about a particular matter or event, the need to use a document may appear. Now, I make that point so that you can put this into perspective. That doesn't mean to say that we will not be alert to the need for documents to be notified in the ordinary course, and if there is a pattern of failure to observe that, the Chamber will certainly act. But this occasion may not justify your comment that this is a pattern. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. It is precisely for this reason that I desisted from interjecting earlier. I take your instructions into account fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, did Mr. Djordjevic or could Mr. Djordjevic make a decision on the dispatching of Special Police units to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija without a previous decision on engagement issued by the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be as brief as possible, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see P1546 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you have already been shown this document. It is a notification from the Bor SUP on a disciplinary procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you to have a look at the last paragraph. It says: "For the above-mentioned reasons, we propose to temporarily remove the sergeant in question from the ministry until the end of disciplinary proceedings, effective as of 23 March 1999." Based on what we can read here, can we conclude that there was a disciplinary procedure instituted against this person?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision that is made by the person in charge of the organisational unit in organisational terms has nothing to do with the initiation of a disciplinary procedure. In other words, one can have simultaneously a disciplinary procedure underway as well as a suspension of the worker in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So is this asking for an approval to have someone suspended?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such an approval is sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Does this have anything to do with a disciplinary procedure and have any disciplinary measures been taken by that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not related to the first issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next please have P356.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you had occasion to see a document in which the minister in a way by dispatch sent instructions on the treatment of the volunteers and paramilitary formations. This is a document dated 18 February 1999. It's a dispatch which came from Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at item 7 which is on the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 7. Does Mr. Djordjevic refer any engagement of volunteers and paramilitary forces in that item?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It only states here that there should be checks carried out of volunteers and paramilitary units. There is no mention of any engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I have some questions for you. You were just asked by counsel if it was possible to dispatch Special Police units to Kosovo without the previous decision or engagement -- or an engagement issued by the minister of the interior himself. And then you asked to be as brief as possible; it was not possible. I appreciate that you wanted to be very short, but could you explain that. What was the reason why this was not possible?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we should deal with legal regulation concerning the Law on Ministries, and Law on State Administration, as well as the Law on the Interior, which are the three principal pieces of legislation governing our work. The only authority lies with the minister of the interior. He is the person empowered to implement those three pieces of legislation. He is a person elected into that position by the Serbian Assembly. All other people were appointed. The minister, however, can delegate certain of his powers to other people. This doesn't need to be specifically a chief of one of the sectors. It can be any of the assistant ministers or chiefs of administrations. So in the context of your question concerning the deployment of PJP units to carry out special security-related tasks in the autonomous province of Kosovo, that decision had to be made by the minister in keeping with the laws I just enumerated. As for all the logistics sending away and reception of those units, these were the tasks to be delegated to any number of persons starting with the various chiefs of administrations, as well as deputy ministers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To avoid any misunderstandings, are you saying that every decision made by any member of the Ministry of the Interior must have been approved by the minister personally before this decision was issued?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such issues were regulated on the rules of work and functioning of the Ministry of the Interior. Those rules specifically enumerate the authority and scope of authority of persons in the seat of the ministry. If, according to the rules, a sector chief was in charge of particular issues, as a rule, the minister did not have to delegate all of his authority to that chief. The issues specified in the rules of the work of the ministry could be applied by the minister in a way he saw fit. He could convey specific aspects of his authority to another person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Another question, I would like to take you back to yesterday, your testimony of yesterday. You told us that the previous -- the former minister, Sokolovic, head deputy minister, he was at the same time the head of the public security. Who was the deputy of Mr. Stojiljkovic, Minister Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, it's not that the minister had assistants or deputies, he had an assistant [as interpreted] minister who at the same time was the chief of the public security sector. However, the principle in place was different. Although, all laws and bylaws remained in power, it depended much on the minister. At the time the minister delegated many of his aspects of authority to the sector and along other professional lines in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to stop you here. Perhaps you misunderstood my question. I wanted to know who stood in for the minister himself? Who was really his deputy of the Minister Stojiljkovic? I'm not talking about assistant ministers.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand you correctly. Are you asking me about a deputy to Minister Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister Stojiljkovic did not have a deputy. He had only assistant ministers and chiefs of sectors, as well as chiefs in charge of specific professional aspects or lines of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My last question, I would like to know about the specific task, what was the duty of Stojan Misic in April 1999 and the MUP. Which was his position?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojan Misic was the assistant minister of the interior directly in charge of those professional aspects which had to do with border affair, administrative affairs, resident aliens, state borders, weapons, fire-fighting department, analyses and IT, as well as communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what was the position of Mr. Zekovic at that time in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Petar Zekovic was the chief the administration; he was also an assistant minister, at the same time in charge of the administration for general affairs. As such, he was in charge of providing accommodation and food supplies for all the employees of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic was assistant minister and the chief of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were all the three assistant ministers on the same level, or were there any differences?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous period there had been less assistants than there are now. In essence an assistant minister is an assistant minister. If a certain assistant is tasked with certain aspects of work, he is answerable solely to the minister. Otherwise, it would have been illogical for chiefs of administrations to be ... Well, we had chiefs of administrations which were answerable for their aspects of work. So as for the role of assistant ministers ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last sentence was not complete.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to say as follows: Why would there have been assistants if there had already been chiefs of administrations in the Ministry of the Interior. Petar Zekovic had already been an administration chief, and at the same time he was assistant minister. Stojan Misic was also an administration chief as well as assistant minister. The fact that he was an assistant minister, it gave him a certain position. And now at the top of the ministry there was a problem, since he was assistant minister in the exercise of control and co-ordination of the lines of work he was in charge with, was directly answerable to the minister. I'm trying to say this, there is a great difference between the rules of systematisation of the ministry and what was taking place in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was one of the three assistant ministers we were talking about subordinate or superior to one of the other of these three assistant ministers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion when assistants are concerned, they were all of the same rank. In my opinion I say. As the chief of a territorial organisational unit, that is to say the chief of the secretariat, I was immediately answerable to the chief of the public security sector. As for any relationships in the ministry itself, that's what needs to be pondered upon. It is my opinion that if we are discussing assistant ministers, they are all directly linked to the minister himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My last question. Did you ever work in the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure whether you are referring to the seat of the ministry. I never worked at the seat of the ministry. I started my career at the Secretariat of the Interior in Valjevo, and I retired following my own request on 30th of December 1991. I have a degree in law, and this is why I was interested in the job systematisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, I was not asking for that, but only if you personally have been employed in the ministry itself and not in the SUP at any time during your career.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never worked in the seat of the ministry as I just said. I only worked in the territorial organisational unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Just one correction in page 35, line 1, in his answer the witness said that the minister had a deputy who was at the same time chief of the public security sector. So not the assistant but the deputy, and this is what may have caused some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that was clarified as the questioning progressed. That concludes the questioning for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and for the assistance you've been able to give. You are, of course, now free to return to your normal activities, and a Court Officer will show you out. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness will be addressed by Mr. Djurdjic. This is witness 6D2, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I take it, Mr. Djurdjic, to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this witness is fully covered by protective measures, so if we could kindly move into a private session. [In english] Closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll actually go into closed session, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
